nodes.name: Space $\ConvH(X)$ of closed convex sets with the Hausdorff metric
nodes.statement: For a Banach space $X$ by $\ConvH(X)$ we denote the space of all non-empty closed convex subsets of $X$, endowed with the {\em Hausdorff metric} $$\dH(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}\dist(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}\dist(b,A)\}\in[0,\infty].$$ Here $\dist(a,B)=\inf\limits_{b\in B}\|a-b\|$ stands for the distance from a point $a\in X$ to a subset $B\subset X$ of the Banach space $X$.
nodes.statement_short: $\ConvH(X)$ is the set of non-empty closed convex subsets of $X$ metrized by the Hausdorff distance $\dH$, valued in $[0,\infty]$.
nodes.genus: the space of all non-empty closed convex subsets of $X$

nodes.name: Hausdorff metric component $\HH_C$
nodes.statement: It is well-known that for each closed convex set $C\in\ConvH(X)$ the Hausdorff distance $\dH$ restricted to the set $$\HH_C=\{A\in\ConvH(X):\dH(A,C)<\infty\}$$is a metric, see \cite[Ch2]{Sendov}. The obtained metric space $(\HH_C,\dH)$ will be called the {\em Hausdorff metric component} (or just {\em component}) of the set $C$ in $\ConvH(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: The component of $C$ is the set of closed convex sets at finite Hausdorff distance from $C$, on which $\dH$ is a genuine metric.

nodes.name: Closed half-space
nodes.statement: {\em a closed half-space} if $C=f^{-1}([a,+\infty)$ for some non-zero linear continuous functional $f:X\to\IR$ and some real number $a\in\IR$;
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C=f^{-1}([a,+\infty)$ for some non-zero linear continuous functional $f:X\to\IR$ and some real number $a\in\IR$

nodes.name: Polyhedral convex set
nodes.statement: {\em polyhedral} if $C$ can be written as the intersection $C=\cap \mathcal F$ of a finite family $\mathcal F$ of closed half-spaces in $X$;
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C$ can be written as the intersection $C=\cap \mathcal F$ of a finite family $\mathcal F$ of closed half-spaces in $X$

nodes.name: Approximatively polyhedral convex set
nodes.statement: {\em approximatively polyhedral} if for every $\e>0$ there is a closed polyhedral subset $P\subset X$ that lies on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C,P)<\e$ from $C$.
nodes.statement_short: $C$ is approximatively polyhedral if polyhedral sets come Hausdorff-arbitrarily close to it.
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: for every $\e>0$ there is a closed polyhedral subset $P\subset X$ that lies on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C,P)<\e$ from $C$

nodes.name: Hiding a set
nodes.statement: Following \cite{BH}, we say that a subset $C$ of a linear space $X$ {\em hides} a set $A\subset X$ if for any two distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]=\{ta+(1-t)b:t\in[0,1]\}$ meets the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: $C$ hides $A$ when every segment joining two distinct points of $A$ crosses $C$.

nodes.name: Hiding convex set
nodes.statement: {\em hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$;
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$

nodes.name: Positively hiding convex set
nodes.statement: {\em positively hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\inf_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)>0$;
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\inf_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)>0$

nodes.name: Infinitely hiding convex set
nodes.statement: {\em infinitely hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)=\infty$.
nodes.genus: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)=\infty$

nodes.name: Density of a topological space; separable space
nodes.statement: Let us recall that the {\em density} $\dens(X)$ of a topological space $X$ is the smallest cardinality $|D|$ of a dense subset $D$ of $X$. Topological spaces with at most countable density are called {\em separable}.
nodes.genus: the smallest cardinality $|D|$ of a dense subset $D$ of $X$

nodes.name: Convex cone
nodes.statement: By a {\em convex cone} in a linear space $X$ we understand a convex subset $C\subset X$ such that $tc\in C$ for any $t\in\bar\IR_+$ and $c\in C$. Here $\bar \IR_+=[0,+\infty)$ stands for the closure of the open half-line $\IR_+=(0,+\infty)$ in $\IR$.

nodes.name: Pointwise sum and homothetic copy of subsets
nodes.statement: For two subsets $A,B$ of a linear space $X$ and a real number $\lambda$, let $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\;b\in B\}$ be the pointwise sum of $A$ and $B$, and $\lambda A=\{\lambda\cdot a:a\in A\}$ be a homothetic copy of $A$.

nodes.name: Cone $\cone(F)$ generated by a subset
nodes.statement: Each subset $F\subset X$ generates the cone $$\cone(F)=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_ix_i:\mbox{$n\in\IN$ and $(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in F^n$, $(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^n\in\bar\IR_+^n$}\Big\},$$which contains the convex hull $\conv(F)$ of $F$.

nodes.name: Characteristic cone $V_C$
nodes.statement: Let us recall that for a convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ its {\em characteristic cone} $V_C$ is defined by $$V_C=\{x\in X:\forall c\in C\;\;c+\bar\IR_+x\subset C\}\subset X.$$
nodes.statement_short: $V_C$ collects the directions along which $C$ contains a whole ray from each of its points.

nodes.name: Dual characteristic cone $V_C^*$
nodes.statement: By the {\em dual characteristic cone} of $C$ we understand the convex cone $$V_C^*=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(C)<\infty\}$$lying in the dual Banach space $X^*$.

nodes.name: Quotient Banach space and quotient operator
nodes.statement: Let us recall that for a Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and a closed linear subspace $Z\subset X$, the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is endowed with the norm $$\|y\|_Y=\inf\big\{\|x\|_X:x\in q^{-1}(y)\big\},$$ where $q:X\to Y$, $q:x\mapsto x+Z$, stands for the quotient operator.

nodes.name: Induced operator $\bar q:\ConvH(X)\to\ConvH(Y)$
nodes.statement: The quotient operator $q:X\to Y$ induces an operator $\bar{q}:\ConvH(X)\to\ConvH(Y)$ assigning to each closed convex set $C\subset X$ the closure $\bar qC$ of its image $qC$ in the Banach space $Y$.

nodes.name: $C$-infinitely hiding convex set
nodes.statement: Let $C_0,C$ be two convex sets in a Banach space $X$. We shall say that $C_0$ is {\em $C$-infinitely hiding} if $C_0$ hides some infinite set $A\subset\aff(C_0)$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: A relative version of infinite hiding: $C_0$ hides an infinite subset of $\aff(C_0)$ that runs infinitely far from $C$.
nodes.genus: two convex sets in a Banach space $X$
differentia: $C_0$ hides some infinite set $A\subset\aff(C_0)$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)=\infty$

nodes.name: Biorthogonal sequence
nodes.statement: We recall that a sequence of pairs $\{(x_n,x^*_n)\}_{n\in \w}\subset X\times X^*$ is {\em biorthogonal} if $x^*_n(x_n)=1$ and $x^*_n(x_k)=0$ for all $n\ne k$, see \cite[1.1]{HMVZ}.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.genus: a sequence of pairs $\{(x_n,x^*_n)\}_{n\in \w}\subset X\times X^*$

nodes.name: Main characterization theorem (Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: For a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is approximatively polyhedral; \item the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\dH(C,V_C)<\infty$; \item the component $\HH_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set; \item the component $\HH_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set; \item the space $\HH_C$ is separable; \item the space $\HH_C$ has density $\dens(\HH_C)<\mathfrak c$. \end{enumerate} If the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional, then the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Approximative polyhedrality of $C$, polyhedrality of $V_C$ at finite distance, and separability (or density $<\mathfrak c$) of the component $\HH_C$ are all equivalent.
assumptions: For a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
If the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional
conclusions: $C$ is approximatively polyhedral;
the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\dH(C,V_C)<\infty$;
the component $\HH_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set;
the component $\HH_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set;
the space $\HH_C$ is separable;
the space $\HH_C$ has density $\dens(\HH_C)<\mathfrak c$.
$C$ is not positively hiding;
$C$ is not infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Hidden characterization of polyhedral convex sets
nodes.statement: By \cite{BH}, a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$ is hiding if and only if $C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull.
nodes.statement_short: A closed convex set in a complete linear metric space hides an infinite set exactly when it fails to be polyhedral in its closed linear hull.
assumptions: a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$
conclusions: is hiding if and only if $C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull

nodes.name: Ramsey Theorem
nodes.statement: The Ramsey Theorem 5 of \cite{Ramsey} yields an infinite subset $\Omega\subset \w$ and a number $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $i(n,m)=i$ and hence $f_i(x_m)>f_i(x_n)+\delta$ for all numbers $n<m$ in $\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: A finite colouring of pairs of naturals admits an infinite monochromatic subset $\Omega$.
nodes.origin_citation: Graham, Rothschild & Spencer, Ramsey Theory (1990), Theorem 5
assumptions: The correspondence $i:(n,m)\to i(n,m)$ can be thought as a finite coloring of the set $[\w]^2=\{(n,m)\in\w^2:n<m\}$ of pairs of positive integers
conclusions: an infinite subset $\Omega\subset \w$ and a number $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $i(n,m)=i$

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach Theorem (weak$^*$ separation form)
nodes.statement: By the Hahn-Banach Theorem applied to the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$, there is an element $x\in X$ that separates $x^*$ from $\cl^*(V^*_C)$ in the sense that $$x^*(x)>\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in\cl^*(V^*_C)\}\ge\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in V^*_C\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: A point outside a weak$^*$-closed convex set can be strictly separated from it by an element of $X$.
assumptions: a functional $x^*\in V^*_{V_C}\setminus\cl^*(V^*_C)$
conclusions: there is an element $x\in X$ that separates $x^*$ from $\cl^*(V^*_C)$

nodes.name: Banach-Alaoglu Theorem
nodes.statement: By the Banach-Alaoglu Theorem this ball is compact in the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
assumptions: the the closed $\frac14$-ball $B^*=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*-x^*_{k}\|\le \frac14\}$ centered at $x^*_{k}$
conclusions: this ball is compact in the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$

nodes.name: Compact convex sets are approximatively polyhedral
nodes.statement: It is well-known that each compact convex subset of Banach space is approximatively polyhedral (see \cite{Gruber} for more information on that topic).
assumptions: each compact convex subset of Banach space
conclusions: is approximatively polyhedral

nodes.name: Hierarchy of hiding properties
nodes.statement: It is clear that each infinitely hiding set is positively hiding and each positively hiding set is hiding.
conclusions: each infinitely hiding set is positively hiding
each positively hiding set is hiding

nodes.name: Dual characteristic cone is closure-invariant
nodes.statement: It is clear that the dual characteristic cone $V_C^*$ of a convex set $C\subset X$ coincides with the dual characteristic cone $V_{\bar C}^*$ of its closure $\bar C$ in $X$.
assumptions: a convex set $C\subset X$
conclusions: the dual characteristic cone $V_C^*$ of a convex set $C\subset X$ coincides with the dual characteristic cone $V_{\bar C}^*$ of its closure $\bar C$ in $X$

nodes.name: Inclusion $V_C^*\subset V^*_{V_C}$ for cones containing zero
nodes.statement: Observe that for a convex $C$ containing zero, the inclusion $V_C\subset C$ implies $V_C^*\subset V^*_{V_C}$.
assumptions: a convex $C$ containing zero
the inclusion $V_C\subset C$
conclusions: $V_C^*\subset V^*_{V_C}$

nodes.name: Infinite hiding equals $C$-infinite hiding
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that a convex set $C\subset X$ is infinitely hiding if and only if it is $C$-infinitely hiding.
assumptions: a convex set $C\subset X$
conclusions: is infinitely hiding if and only if it is $C$-infinitely hiding

nodes.name: Classical description of polyhedral cones and polyhedral convex sets
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional Banach space. \begin{enumerate} \item A convex cone $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\cone(F)$ for some finite set $F\subset X$. \item A convex set $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\cone(F)+\conv(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: In finite dimensions polyhedral cones are exactly finitely generated cones, and polyhedral convex sets are exactly $\cone(F)+\conv(E)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Klee 1959; Ziegler, Lectures on Polytopes, Thms 1.2-1.3; Gallier, Notes on Convex Sets, S4.3
assumptions: Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional Banach space.
conclusions: A convex cone $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\cone(F)$ for some finite set $F\subset X$.
A convex set $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\cone(F)+\conv(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$.

nodes.name: Characteristic cone versus characteristic cone of the closure
nodes.statement: Let $\bar C$ be the closure of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$. Then \begin{enumerate} \item $V_C\subset V_{\bar C}$; \item $V_C=V_{\bar C}$ if the set $C$ is open in $X$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $\bar C$ be the closure of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$.
conclusions: $V_C\subset V_{\bar C}$
$V_C=V_{\bar C}$ if the set $C$ is open in $X$

nodes.name: Prescribed distance along a non-recession direction
nodes.statement: For each point $c_0$ of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$, each vector $v\notin V_{\bar C}$ and each real number $\e\in\IR_+$ there is a real number $t\in\IR_+$ such that $\dist(c_0+tv,C)=\e$.
nodes.statement_short: Along a direction outside $V_{\bar C}$ the distance to $C$ attains every prescribed positive value.
assumptions: For each point $c_0$ of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$
each vector $v\notin V_{\bar C}$
each real number $\e\in\IR_+$
conclusions: there is a real number $t\in\IR_+$ such that $\dist(c_0+tv,C)=\e$

nodes.name: Finite Hausdorff distance implies equal characteristic cones
nodes.statement: Let $A,B$ be two closed convex sets in a Banach space $X$. If $\dH(A,B)<\infty$, then $V_A=V_B$.
assumptions: Let $A,B$ be two closed convex sets in a Banach space $X$.
$\dH(A,B)<\infty$
conclusions: $V_A=V_B$

nodes.name: Dual characteristic cone of the characteristic cone
nodes.statement: For any closed convex set $C$ in a Banach space the dual characteristic cone $V^*_{V_C}$ of the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ coincides with the weak$^*$ closure $\cl^*(V_C)$ of $V_C$.
nodes.statement_short: $V^*_{V_C}$ is exactly the weak$^*$ closure of the dual characteristic cone.
assumptions: For any closed convex set $C$ in a Banach space
conclusions: the dual characteristic cone $V^*_{V_C}$ of the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ coincides with the weak$^*$ closure $\cl^*(V_C)$ of $V_C$

nodes.name: Polyhedral set lies at finite distance from its characteristic cone
nodes.statement: For a normed space $X$, functionals $f_1,\dots,f_n:X\to\IR$, a vector $\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\IR^n$ with non-negative coordinates, and the polyhedral convex set $$P_{\mathbf a}=\bigcap\limits_{i=1}^nf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$$ \begin{enumerate} \item the characteristic cone $V_{P_{\mathbf a}}$ of the convex set $P_{\mathbf a}$ coincides with the polyhedral cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$; \item $\dH(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le \dH(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})\cdot\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$, \end{enumerate} where $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: The characteristic cone of $P_{\mathbf a}$ is $P_{\mathbf 0}$, and $\dH(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})$ is controlled linearly by $\max_i a_i$.
assumptions: For a normed space $X$
a vector $\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\IR^n$ with non-negative coordinates
P_{\mathbf a}=\bigcap\limits_{i=1}^nf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)
conclusions: the characteristic cone $V_{P_{\mathbf a}}$ of the convex set $P_{\mathbf a}$ coincides with the polyhedral cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$
$\dH(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le \dH(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})\cdot\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$

nodes.name: Countable dense family of polyhedra (finite-dimensional case)
nodes.statement: If the component $\HH_C$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a finite-dimensional Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set, then $\HH_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral convex sets.
nodes.statement_short: In finite dimensions, one polyhedral set in $\HH_C$ forces a countable dense family of polyhedra in $\HH_C$.
assumptions: the component $\HH_C$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a finite-dimensional Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set
conclusions: $\HH_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral convex sets

nodes.name: Quotient operator preserves closedness, polyhedrality and $\dH$
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a closed linear subspace of a Banach space $X$, $Y=X/Z$ be the quotient Banach space, and $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator. \begin{enumerate} \item A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is closed in $X$ if and only if the image $qC$ is closed in $Y$. \item A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ if and only if its image $qC$ is polyhedral in $Y$. \item For any non-empty convex sets $A,B\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_A\cap V_B$ we get $\dH(A,B)=\dH(qA,qB)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $Z$ be a closed linear subspace of a Banach space $X$, $Y=X/Z$ be the quotient Banach space, and $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator.
conclusions: A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is closed in $X$ if and only if the image $qC$ is closed in $Y$.
A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ if and only if its image $qC$ is polyhedral in $Y$.
For any non-empty convex sets $A,B\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_A\cap V_B$ we get $\dH(A,B)=\dH(qA,qB)$.

nodes.name: Countable dense family of polyhedra (Banach case)
nodes.statement: If the component $\HH_C$ of a non-empty closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set, then $\HH_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral closed sets, which implies that the space $\HH_C$ is separable and the convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral.
nodes.statement_short: One polyhedral set in $\HH_C$ makes $\HH_C$ separable and $C$ approximatively polyhedral, in any Banach space.
assumptions: the component $\HH_C$ of a non-empty closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set
conclusions: $\HH_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral closed sets
the space $\HH_C$ is separable and the convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral

nodes.name: Hiding is inherited by convex hulls
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a convex subset of a linear space $X$ and $a,b\in X$ two points such that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$. Then for any points $x\in\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ and $y\in\conv(X\cup\{b\})$ we get $[x,y]\cap C\ne\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: If $[a,b]$ meets $C$, then so does every segment joining $\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ to $\conv(C\cup\{b\})$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a convex subset of a linear space $X$ and $a,b\in X$ two points such that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$.
any points $x\in\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ and $y\in\conv(X\cup\{b\})$
conclusions: $[x,y]\cap C\ne\emptyset$

nodes.name: Positively hiding sets force density $\ge\mathfrak c$
nodes.statement: The component $\HH_C\subset\ConvH(X)$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ has density $\dens(\HH_C)\ge\mathfrak c$ provided $\HH_C$ contains a positively hiding closed convex subset $P$ of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: A positively hiding member of $\HH_C$ makes the component have density at least continuum.
assumptions: a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
$\HH_C$ contains a positively hiding closed convex subset $P$ of $X$
conclusions: $\dens(\HH_C)\ge\mathfrak c$

nodes.name: Hiding cone sections are $C$-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure. For a linear subspace $Z\subset X$, the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is $C$-infinitely hiding if the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is a hiding convex set in $Z$.
assumptions: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure.
the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is a hiding convex set in $Z$
conclusions: the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is $C$-infinitely hiding

nodes.name: Non-polyhedral cone sections are $C$-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure. For a closed linear subspace $Z\subset X$ the intersection $V=Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is infinitely $C$-hiding if the cone $V$ is polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V^\pm=\cl(V-V)$.
assumptions: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure.
For a closed linear subspace $Z\subset X$
the cone $V$ is polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V^\pm=\cl(V-V)$
conclusions: the intersection $V=Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is infinitely $C$-hiding

nodes.name: Non-polyhedral characteristic cone implies infinite hiding
nodes.statement: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space is infinitely hiding if its characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V_C^\pm=\cl(V_C-V_C)$.
assumptions: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space
its characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V_C^\pm=\cl(V_C-V_C)$
conclusions: $C$ of a Banach space is infinitely hiding

nodes.name: Lifting hidden sets through a linear operator
nodes.statement: Let $q:X\to \tilde X$ be a linear operator between linear spaces, $E=q^{-1}(0)$ be the kernel of $q$, and $C\subset X$ be a convex set such that $V_{C\cap E}-V_{C\cap E}=E$. If the image $\tilde C=q(C)$ hides some countable set $\tilde A\subset \aff(\tilde C)$, then $C$ hides some set $A\subset \aff(C)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$.
nodes.statement_short: A countable set hidden by the image $q(C)$ lifts to a set hidden by $C$, provided $V_{C\cap E}-V_{C\cap E}=E$ on the kernel.
assumptions: Let $q:X\to \tilde X$ be a linear operator between linear spaces, $E=q^{-1}(0)$ be the kernel of $q$, and $C\subset X$ be a convex set such that $V_{C\cap E}-V_{C\cap E}=E$.
the image $\tilde C=q(C)$ hides some countable set $\tilde A\subset \aff(\tilde C)$
conclusions: $C$ hides some set $A\subset \aff(C)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$

nodes.name: Quotient version of $C$-infinite hiding
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a Banach space, $E$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space and $q:X\to \tilde X$ be the quotient operator. Let $C_0,C$ be two convex sets in $X$ and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, $\tilde C=q(C)$ be their quotient images in $\tilde X$. The convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding $X$ if its image $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding and $E=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$.

Then the polyhedral convex set $C_F=\conv(F)+P$ lies on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_F,A_r)<\e$ from the set $A_r$ and hence on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_F,A)\le \dH(C_F,A_r)+\dH(A_r,A)<2\e$ from $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $P$ to the polyhedral cone $V_C=\cone(B)$, take the countable family $C_F=\conv(F)+V_C$ over finite $F$ in a dense $D$, and approximate any $A\in\HH_C$ via a bounded truncation.

nodes.name: Dispose of the trivial case and normalize $P$
nodes.statement: The case $C=X$ is trivial because in this case the component $\HH_C=\{X\}$ contains a unique convex set $X$, which is polyhedral as the intersection of the empty family of closed half-spaces. So, we assume that $\HH_C$ contains some polyhedral convex set $P\ne X$. Without loss of generality we can assume that $0\in P$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}, $\dH(C,P)<\infty$ implies $V_C=V_P\ne X$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $C\ne X$, $0\in P$, and note $V_C=V_P\ne X$ by Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Reduce $P$ to a polyhedral cone generated by a finite set
nodes.statement: Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\IR$ are linear continuous functionals with unit norm and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are some real numbers. It follows from $0\in P$ that $a_1,\dots,a_n\ge 0$. According to Lemma~\ref{l2.6}, we lose no generality assuming that $a_1=\dots=a_k=0$, which implies that $P$ is a polyhedral cone that coincides with its characteristic cone $V_P=V_C$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.1}, $P=\cone(B)$ for some finite subset $B\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemmas 2.6 and 2.1 one may assume $P=V_P=V_C=\cone(B)$ for a finite $B$.

nodes.name: Build the countable candidate family
nodes.statement: By our assumption, the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional and hence separable. So, we can fix a countable dense subset $D\subset X$. Next, for every finite subset $F\subset D$ consider its convex hull $\conv(F)$ and the polyhedral convex set $$C_F=\conv(F)+V_C=\conv(F)+\cone(B).$$ It remains to check that the countable family $$\mathcal C=\{C_F:\mbox{$F$ is a finite subset of $D$}\}$$ is dense in $\HH_C$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a countable dense $D\subset X$ and set $C_F=\conv(F)+V_C$ for finite $F\subset D$.

nodes.name: Set up the approximation target
nodes.statement: Given a convex set $A\in\HH$ and $\e>0$, we shall find a finite subset $F\subset D$ with $\dH(C_F,A)< 2\e$. Denote by $\bar \IB=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$ the closed unit ball of the Banach space $X$. Then for every $r>0$ the set $r\bar\IB=\{r\cdot x:x\in\bar\IB\}$ coincides with the closed $r$-ball $\{x\in X:\|x\|\le r\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Given $A\in\HH_C$ and $\e>0$, aim for $F$ with $\dH(C_F,A)<2\e$.

nodes.name: Combine the truncation claim with compact approximation
nodes.statement: Claim~\ref{cl3.2} yields us a real number $r\in\IR_+$ such that the intersection $A\cap r\bar\IB$ is not empty and $\dist(A_r,A)<\e$ where $A_r=(A\cap r\bar\IB)+P$. By \cite{Gruber}, the compact convex set $A\cap r\bar\IB$ can be approximated by a finite subset $F\subset D$ such that $\dH(\conv(F),A\cap r\bar \IB)<\e$. Then the polyhedral convex set $C_F=\conv(F)+P$ lies on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_F,A_r)<\e$ from the set $A_r$ and hence on Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_F,A)\le \dH(C_F,A_r)+\dH(A_r,A)<2\e$ from $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the compact set $A\cap r\bar\IB$ by $\conv(F)$ and add the two $\e$-errors.

nodes.statement: It follows from $\dH(A,C)<\infty$ that $V_A=V_C=P$, see Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}. Then for each $r\in\IR_+$ we get the inclusion $$A_r=(A\cap r\bar\IB)+P\subset A+P=A+V_A=A.$$

nodes.statement: Assuming that $\dH(A_r,A)>\e$ for all $r\in\IR_+$, we can construct an increasing sequence of positive real numbers $(r_n)_{n\in\w}$ and a sequence of points $(x_n)_{n\in\w}$ in $A$ such that $\|x_n\|\le r_n$ and $\dist(x_{n+1},A_{r_{n}})>\e$ for all $n\in\w$. nodes.name: Apply Ramsey and contradict boundedness of $f_i$ on $C$
nodes.statement: The correspondence $i:(n,m)\to i(n,m)$ can be thought as a finite coloring of the set $[\w]^2=\{(n,m)\in\w^2:n<m\}$ of pairs of positive integers. The Ramsey Theorem 5 of \cite{Ramsey} yields an infinite subset $\Omega\subset \w$ and a number $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $i(n,m)=i$ and hence $f_i(x_m)>f_i(x_n)+\delta$ for all numbers $n<m$ in $\Omega$. nodes.statement_short: A monochromatic infinite $\Omega$ makes $\sup f_i(C)=\infty$, contradicting $\dH(C,P)<\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Countable dense family of polyhedra (Banach case)
nodes.statement: The statement of the lemma is trivial if $C=X$. So, we assume that $C\ne X$ and $\HH_C$ contains a polyhedral convex set $P$. Replacing $P$ by its shift, we can assume that $0\in P$. Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big),$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\IR$ are suitable linear continuous functionals and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are suitable non-negative real numbers. It follows from $\dH(C,P)<\infty$ that the characteristic cone $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$ is polyhedral and the closed linear subspace $$Z=-V_C\cap V_C=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}(0)$$has finite codimension in $X$. Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is finite-dimensional. Taking into account that $Z\subset V_P\cap V_C$ and applying Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1,3), we conclude that the images $qC$ and $qP$ are closed convex sets in $Y$ with $\dH(qC,qP)<\infty$. Moreover, the convex set $qP$ is polyhedral in $Y$. Since the Banach space $Y$ is finite-dimensional, it is legal to apply Lemma~\ref{l3.1} in order to find a dense countable subset $\mathcal D_Y\in\HH_{qC}$ that consists of polyhedral convex sets. By Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(2), the countable family $\mathcal D_X=\{q^{-1}(D):D\in\mathcal D_X\}$ consists of polyhedral convex subsets of $X$ and by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(3) is dense in the component $\HH_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient by the lineality space $Z$ of $V_C$ to land in a finite-dimensional $Y$, apply Lemma 3.1 there, and pull the countable dense family back through $q$.

nodes.name: Trivial case and normalization
nodes.statement: The statement of the lemma is trivial if $C=X$. So, we assume that $C\ne X$ and $\HH_C$ contains a polyhedral convex set $P$. Replacing $P$ by its shift, we can assume that $0\in P$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $C\ne X$ and $0\in P$ for a polyhedral $P\in\HH_C$.

nodes.name: Identify the finite-codimensional lineality subspace
nodes.statement: Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big),$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\IR$ are suitable linear continuous functionals and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are suitable non-negative real numbers. It follows from $\dH(C,P)<\infty$ that the characteristic cone $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$ is polyhedral and the closed linear subspace $$Z=-V_C\cap V_C=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}(0)$$has finite codimension in $X$.
nodes.statement_short: $V_C=V_P$ is polyhedral and $Z=-V_C\cap V_C$ has finite codimension.

nodes.name: Transfer to the finite-dimensional quotient and pull back
nodes.statement: Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is finite-dimensional. Taking into account that $Z\subset V_P\cap V_C$ and applying Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1,3), we conclude that the images $qC$ and $qP$ are closed convex sets in $Y$ with $\dH(qC,qP)<\infty$. Moreover, the convex set $qP$ is polyhedral in $Y$. Since the Banach space $Y$ is finite-dimensional, it is legal to apply Lemma~\ref{l3.1} in order to find a dense countable subset $\mathcal D_Y\in\HH_{qC}$ that consists of polyhedral convex sets. By Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(2), the countable family $\mathcal D_X=\{q^{-1}(D):D\in\mathcal D_X\}$ consists of polyhedral convex subsets of $X$ and by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(3) is dense in the component $\HH_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.1 in $Y=X/Z$ and lift the countable dense family by $q^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Hiding is inherited by convex hulls
nodes.statement: The lemma trivially holds if $x$ or $y$ belongs to the set $C$. So, we assume that $x,y\notin C$. It follows that the point $x\in\conv(C\cup\{a\})\setminus C$ can be written as $x=t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x$ for some $t_x\in(0,1]$ and $c_x\in C$. The same is true for the point $y\in\conv(C\cup\{b\})\setminus C$ which can be written as $y=t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y$ for some $t_y\in(0,1]$ and $c_y\in C$. By our assumption, the intersection $[a,b]\cap C$ contains some point $c=ta+(1-t)b$ where $t\in[0,1]$. The lemma will be proved as soon as we check that the segment $[x,y]$ meets the convex hull $\conv(\{c,c_x,c_y\})\subset C$ of the 3-element set $\{c,c_x,c_y\}\subset C$. This will follow as soon as we find real numbers $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y\in[0,1]$ such that $\alpha+\alpha_x+\alpha_y=1$ and $$\alpha c+\alpha_xc_x+\alpha_yc_y=ux+(1-u)y=u(t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x)+(1-u)(t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y).$$ The number $u\in[0,1]$ can be found from the equation $$ut_xa+(1-u)t_yb=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)(ta+(1-t)b)=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)c,$$ which has a well-defined solution $$u=\frac{t\cdot t_y}{t\cdot t_y+(1-t)t_x}.$$ The remaining numbers $\alpha,\alpha_x$ and $\alpha_y$ can be found as $$\alpha=ut_x+(1-u)t_y,\quad \alpha_x=u(1-t_x),\quad\alpha_y=(1-u)(1-t_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Write $x,y$ as convex combinations involving $a,b$ and solve explicitly for barycentric coefficients placing a point of $[x,y]$ in $\conv(\{c,c_x,c_y\})\subset C$.

nodes.name: Represent $x$ as a convex combination
nodes.statement: The lemma trivially holds if $x$ or $y$ belongs to the set $C$. So, we assume that $x,y\notin C$. It follows that the point $x\in\conv(C\cup\{a\})\setminus C$ can be written as $x=t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x$ for some $t_x\in(0,1]$ and $c_x\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x=t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x$ with $c_x\in C$.

nodes.name: Represent $y$ similarly
nodes.statement: The same is true for the point $y\in\conv(C\cup\{b\})\setminus C$ which can be written as $y=t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y$ for some $t_y\in(0,1]$ and $c_y\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $y=t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y$ with $c_y\in C$.

nodes.name: Use the hypothesis on $[a,b]$
nodes.statement: By our assumption, the intersection $[a,b]\cap C$ contains some point $c=ta+(1-t)b$ where $t\in[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $c=ta+(1-t)b$ in $[a,b]\cap C$.

nodes.name: Reduce to solving a barycentric identity
nodes.statement: The lemma will be proved as soon as we check that the segment $[x,y]$ meets the convex hull $\conv(\{c,c_x,c_y\})\subset C$ of the 3-element set $\{c,c_x,c_y\}\subset C$. This will follow as soon as we find real numbers $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y\in[0,1]$ such that $\alpha+\alpha_x+\alpha_y=1$ and $$\alpha c+\alpha_xc_x+\alpha_yc_y=ux+(1-u)y=u(t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x)+(1-u)(t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to find $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y$ matching a point of $[x,y]$ with $\conv(\{c,c_x,c_y\})$.

nodes.name: Solve for the coefficients
nodes.statement: The number $u\in[0,1]$ can be found from the equation $$ut_xa+(1-u)t_yb=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)(ta+(1-t)b)=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)c,$$ which has a well-defined solution $$u=\frac{t\cdot t_y}{t\cdot t_y+(1-t)t_x}.$$ The remaining numbers $\alpha,\alpha_x$ and $\alpha_y$ can be found as $$\alpha=ut_x+(1-u)t_y,\quad \alpha_x=u(1-t_x),\quad\alpha_y=(1-u)(1-t_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formulas for $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y$ finish the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Positively hiding sets force density $\ge\mathfrak c$
nodes.statement: Since $\HH_C=\HH_P$, we lose no generality assuming that the convex set $C$ itself is positively hiding, which means that there is an infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ on positive distance $\e=\inf_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)$ from $C$, which is hidden behind the set $C$ in the sense that for any distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. Fix any point $c_0\in C$ and for every point $a\in A$ choose a point $b_a\in[c_0,a]$ on the distance $\dist(b_a,C)=\e$ from $C$. The choice of the point $b_a$ is possible as $\dist(a,C)\ge\e$. Lemma~\ref{l4.1} guarantees that the set $B=\{b_a:a\in A\}$ is infinite and is hidden behind the set $C$. Moreover, this set lies in the $2\e$-neighborhood $C+2\e\IB$ of $C$. Here $\IB=\{x\in X:\|x\|< 1\}$ stands for the open unit ball in the Banach space $X$. Now for any subset $\beta\subset B$ consider the convex set $C_\beta=\conv(C\cup\beta)$. Applying Lemma~\ref{l4.1} one can show that this set is closed in $X$ and $C_\beta=\bigcup_{b\in\beta}\conv(C\cup\{b\})$. Taking into account that $C\subset C_\beta\subset C+2\e\IB$, we see that $\dH(C,C_\beta)\le 2\e$ and hence $C_\beta$ belongs to the component $\HH_C$ of $C$. We claim that for any two distinct subsets $\alpha,\beta\subset B$, the convex sets $C_\alpha$ and $C_\beta$ lie on the Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_\alpha,C_\beta)\ge\e$. Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, there is a point $b\in (\beta\setminus\alpha)\cup(\alpha\setminus\beta)$. We lose no generality assuming that $b\in\beta\setminus\alpha$. Then $b\in C_\beta$ and $\dist(b,C_\alpha)\ge\e$. Indeed, assuming that $\dist(b,C_\alpha)<\e$, we conclude that the open $\e$-ball $b+\e\IB$ meets the set $C_\alpha=\conv(C\cup\alpha)=\bigcup_{a\in \alpha}\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ at some point $x$ that belongs to $\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ for some point $a\in\alpha$. Since the set $B\ni a,b$ is hidden behind the set $C$, the segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. By Lemma~\ref{l4.1}, the segment $[x,b]$ also meets the set $C$, which is not possible as $[x,b]$ lies in the $\e$-ball $b+\e \IB$, which does not meet $C$ as $\dist(b,C)=\e$. This contradiction shows that $\dist(b,C_\alpha)\ge\e$ and hence $\dH(C_\beta,C_\alpha)\ge\e$. Now we see that the component $\HH_C$ contains the subset $\mathcal C=\{C_\beta:\beta\subset B\}$ of cardinality $|\mathcal C|\ge 2^{|B|}\ge\mathfrak c$, consisting of points on mutual distance $\ge \e$. This implies that $\dens(\HH_C)\ge |\mathcal C|\ge \mathfrak c$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull the hidden set to distance exactly $\e$, then the $2^{|B|}$ sets $C_\beta=\conv(C\cup\beta)$ are pairwise $\e$-separated points of $\HH_C$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $C$ itself positively hiding
nodes.statement: Since $\HH_C=\HH_P$, we lose no generality assuming that the convex set $C$ itself is positively hiding, which means that there is an infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ on positive distance $\e=\inf_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)$ from $C$, which is hidden behind the set $C$ in the sense that for any distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $C$ hides an infinite $A$ at distance $\ge\e>0$.

nodes.name: Move the hidden set to distance exactly $\e$
nodes.statement: Fix any point $c_0\in C$ and for every point $a\in A$ choose a point $b_a\in[c_0,a]$ on the distance $\dist(b_a,C)=\e$ from $C$. The choice of the point $b_a$ is possible as $\dist(a,C)\ge\e$. Lemma~\ref{l4.1} guarantees that the set $B=\{b_a:a\in A\}$ is infinite and is hidden behind the set $C$. Moreover, this set lies in the $2\e$-neighborhood $C+2\e\IB$ of $C$. Here $\IB=\{x\in X:\|x\|< 1\}$ stands for the open unit ball in the Banach space $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $A$ by $B=\{b_a\}$ with $\dist(b_a,C)=\e$, still hidden by Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Form the family of convex hulls
nodes.statement: Now for any subset $\beta\subset B$ consider the convex set $C_\beta=\conv(C\cup\beta)$. Applying Lemma~\ref{l4.1} one can show that this set is closed in $X$ and $C_\beta=\bigcup_{b\in\beta}\conv(C\cup\{b\})$. Taking into account that $C\subset C_\beta\subset C+2\e\IB$, we see that $\dH(C,C_\beta)\le 2\e$ and hence $C_\beta$ belongs to the component $\HH_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\beta\subset B$ the set $C_\beta=\conv(C\cup\beta)$ lies in $\HH_C$.

nodes.name: Show the family is $\e$-separated
nodes.statement: We claim that for any two distinct subsets $\alpha,\beta\subset B$, the convex sets $C_\alpha$ and $C_\beta$ lie on the Hausdorff distance $\dH(C_\alpha,C_\beta)\ge\e$. Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, there is a point $b\in (\beta\setminus\alpha)\cup(\alpha\setminus\beta)$. We lose no generality assuming that $b\in\beta\setminus\alpha$. Then $b\in C_\beta$ and $\dist(b,C_\alpha)\ge\e$. Indeed, assuming that $\dist(b,C_\alpha)<\e$, we conclude that the open $\e$-ball $b+\e\IB$ meets the set $C_\alpha=\conv(C\cup\alpha)=\bigcup_{a\in \alpha}\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ at some point $x$ that belongs to $\conv(C\cup\{a\})$ for some point $a\in\alpha$. Since the set $B\ni a,b$ is hidden behind the set $C$, the segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. By Lemma~\ref{l4.1}, the segment $[x,b]$ also meets the set $C$, which is not possible as $[x,b]$ lies in the $\e$-ball $b+\e \IB$, which does not meet $C$ as $\dist(b,C)=\e$. This contradiction shows that $\dist(b,C_\alpha)\ge\e$ and hence $\dH(C_\beta,C_\alpha)\ge\e$.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct $\alpha,\beta$ give $\dH(C_\alpha,C_\beta)\ge\e$, via Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Count and conclude
nodes.statement: Now we see that the component $\HH_C$ contains the subset $\mathcal C=\{C_\beta:\beta\subset B\}$ of cardinality $|\mathcal C|\ge 2^{|B|}\ge\mathfrak c$, consisting of points on mutual distance $\ge \e$. This implies that $\dens(\HH_C)\ge |\mathcal C|\ge \mathfrak c$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuum many $\e$-separated points force $\dens(\HH_C)\ge\mathfrak c$.

nodes.name: Proof of Hiding cone sections are $C$-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Assume that the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ hides some infinite injectively enumerated set $\{a_n\}_{n\in\w}\subset Z\setminus V_{\bar C}$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.3}, for every $n\in\w$, there is a real number $t_n>0$ such that $\dist(t_n a_n,C)>n$. It is clear that for the set $A=\{t_na_n\}_{n\in\w}$ we get $\sup\limits_{a\in A}\dist(a,C)=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\dist(t_na_n,C)=\infty$. It remains to show that for every distinct numbers $n,m\in\w$ the segment $[t_na_n,t_mb_m]$ intersects the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$. nodes.statement:
This lemma will be proved by induction on the dimension $\dim(Z)$ of $Z$. The lemma is trivially true if $\dim(Z)\le 1$. Assume that the lemma has been proved for all triples $(X,C,Z)$ with $\dim(Z)<n$. Now we prove this lemma for $\dim(Z)=n$. Assuming that $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$, we need to prove that the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding. To derive a contradiction, assume that $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding. In this case Lemma~ef{l5.6} implies the following fact, which will be used several times in the subsequent proof.  egin{claim} For each two-dimensional linear subspace $Z_2\subset Z$ we get $\dH(Z_2\cap C_0,V_{Z_2\cap C_0})<\infty$. \end{claim} Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{ ar C_0}$ of the open convex set $C_0$ in $Z$.  egin{claim} The linear subspace $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is trivial. \end{claim}  egin{proof} Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$. Consider the quotient Banach space $	ilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X	o 	ilde X$, the convex set $	ilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $	ilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(	ilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z	o	ilde Z$ is open, the convex set $	ilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $	ilde Z$ and hence the convex set $	ilde Z\cap	ilde C$ has non-empty interior in $	ilde Z$. Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $	ilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $	ilde X$ by Lemma~ef{l3.3}(1). nodes.name: Set up the induction and the contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement: This lemma will be proved by induction on the dimension $\dim(Z)$ of $Z$. The lemma is trivially true if $\dim(Z)\le 1$. Assume that the lemma has been proved for all triples $(X,C,Z)$ with $\dim(Z)<n$. Now we prove this lemma for $\dim(Z)=n$. Assuming that $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$, we need to prove that the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding. To derive a contradiction, assume that $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding. In this case Lemma~\ref{l5.6} implies the following fact, which will be used several times in the subsequent proof.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $\dim(Z)$ and assume $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding, which yields Claim 5.8.

nodes.name: Introduce the characteristic cone of the section
nodes.statement: Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{\bar C_0}$ of the open convex set $C_0$ in $Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Bring in $V_{C_0}$ before establishing its lineality and dimension.

nodes.name: Write $V_{C_0}$ as a minimal polyhedral intersection
nodes.statement: Since $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding, Lemma~\ref{l5.2}, guarantees that the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}$ is polyhedral in $Z$ and hence it can be written as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$V_{C_0}=\bigcap_{i=1}^k f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$determined by some linear functionals $f_1,\dots,f_k:Z\to\IR$. We shall assume that the number $k$ in this representation is the smallest possible.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.2 makes $V_{C_0}$ polyhedral; fix a minimal half-space representation.

nodes.name: Locate an unbounded functional
nodes.statement: It follows from $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ and Lemma~\ref{l2.6} that $\sup f_i(C_0)=\infty$ for some $i\le k$.
nodes.statement_short: Some $f_i$ is unbounded above on $C_0$.

nodes.name: Quotient by the line spanned by the face vector
nodes.statement: Claim~\ref{cl5.11} yields a non-zero vector $e\in f_i^{-1}(0)\cap V_{C_0}$. Consider the 1-dimensional linear subspace $E=\IR e$ of $X$ and let $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space. Observe that $\tilde X$ contains the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=Z/E$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)=\dim(Z)-1<n$. Let $q:X\to\tilde X$ be the quotient operator, and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, $\tilde C=q(C)$ be the images of the convex sets $C_0$ and $C$ in $\tilde X$. It follows from $E=q^{-1}(0)\subset Z$ that $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C=q(Z\cap C)$ and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ coincides with the interior of the set $q(Z\cap C)=\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ in $\tilde Z$. So, the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde Z,\tilde C)$ satisfies the assumptions of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $E=\IR e$ to drop the dimension while keeping the hypotheses.

nodes.name: Factor $f_i$ through the quotient
nodes.statement: We claim that $\dH(\tilde C_0,V_{\tilde C_0})=\infty$. Since $E\subset f_i^{-1}(0)$, there is a linear functional $\tilde f_i:\tilde Z\to \IR$ such that $f_i=\tilde f_i\circ q|Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $E\subset f_i^{-1}(0)$, $f_i$ descends to $\tilde f_i$ on $\tilde Z$.

nodes.name: Apply the inductive hypothesis and contradict
nodes.statement: Taking into account that $\infty=\sup f_i(C_0)=\sup \tilde f_i(\tilde C_0)$, we conclude that $\dH(\tilde C_0,V_{\tilde C_0})=\infty$ and by the inductive assumption, the open convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding (as $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$). Since $E=\IR_+e-\IR_+e=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. This contradiction completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{l5.7}.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding by induction, so Lemma 5.4 contradicts the assumption.

nodes.name: Proof of Lineality space of $V_{C_0}$ is trivial
nodes.statement: Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$. Consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$, the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z\to\tilde Z$ is open, the convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $\tilde Z$ and hence the convex set $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ has non-empty interior in $\tilde Z$. Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $\tilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $\tilde X$ by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1). Now we can see that the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde C,\tilde Z)$ satisfies the requirements of Lemma~\ref{l5.7} with $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. So, by the inductive assumption, the convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding. Since $E=V_{E\cap C_0}=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. But this contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: A non-trivial lineality space would let the inductive hypothesis apply to the smaller quotient and, via Lemma 5.4, make $C_0$ $C$-infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Quotient by the lineality space and apply induction
nodes.statement: Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$. Consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$, the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z\to\tilde Z$ is open, the convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $\tilde Z$ and hence the convex set $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ has non-empty interior in $\tilde Z$. Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $\tilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $\tilde X$ by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1). Now we can see that the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde C,\tilde Z)$ satisfies the requirements of Lemma~\ref{l5.7} with $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. So, by the inductive assumption, the convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: If $E\ne\{0\}$, the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde C,\tilde Z)$ has smaller dimension, so induction applies.

nodes.name: Pull the property back and contradict
nodes.statement: Since $E=V_{E\cap C_0}=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. But this contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.4 transfers $C$-infinite hiding back to $C_0$, contradicting the standing assumption.

nodes.name: Proof of $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that $\dim(V_{C_0})\le 1$. The equality $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ is unbounded in the finite-dimensional linear space $Z\cap C_0$ and consequently $V_{C_0}\ne 0$. Since $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}=\{0\}$, we conclude that $V_{C_0}=\bar\IR_+ e$ for some non-zero vector $e\in V_{C_0}$. Now consider the linear subspace $E=\IR e\subset Z$, the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$, the convex sets $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the open convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, which is dense in $\tilde C$. Claim~\ref{cl5.8} guarantees that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone and hence is bounded in the finite-dimensional space $\tilde Z$. This implies that $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$, which is a desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: A cone of dimension $\le 1$ would make the quotient section bounded, forcing $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$.

nodes.name: Reduce to a single ray
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that $\dim(V_{C_0})\le 1$. The equality $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ is unbounded in the finite-dimensional linear space $Z\cap C_0$ and consequently $V_{C_0}\ne 0$. Since $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}=\{0\}$, we conclude that $V_{C_0}=\bar\IR_+ e$ for some non-zero vector $e\in V_{C_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial lineality plus unboundedness force $V_{C_0}=\bar\IR_+e$.

nodes.name: Quotient by that ray and contradict
nodes.statement: Now consider the linear subspace $E=\IR e\subset Z$, the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$, the convex sets $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the open convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, which is dense in $\tilde C$. Claim~\ref{cl5.8} guarantees that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone and hence is bounded in the finite-dimensional space $\tilde Z$. This implies that $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$, which is a desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.8 makes $\tilde C_0$ bounded, so $\dH(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$.

nodes.statement: Since $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$, there exists a vector $y\in V_{C_0}\setminus\IR x$. Such choice of $x$ guarantees that $0\notin [x,y]$. nodes.name: Proof of $V_{\tilde C_0}\subset \tilde f_i^{-1}(-\infty,0]$
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some vector $w\in \tilde Z$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$. Then $\IR_+w\subset \tilde Z$. Pick any vector $v\in q^{-1}(w)\subset Z$ and consider the two-dimensional subspace $Z_2=\lin(\{v,e\})$ spanning the vectors $v$ and $e$. Observe that for every $t\in\IR$ we get $f_i(v+te)=\tilde f_i(w)>0$, which implies that $(v+t\IR)\cap V_{Z_2\cap C}=\emptyset$. Then $V_{Z_2\cap C}\subset \IR e-\bar\IR_+v$ and $q(V_{Z_2\cap C})\subset -\bar\IR_+w$. On the other hand, the projection $q(Z_2\cap C)$ contains the half-line $\IR_+ w$, which implies that $\dH(Z_2\cap C,V_{Z_2\cap C})=\infty$. But this contradicts Claim~\ref{cl5.8}.
nodes.statement_short: A vector $w$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$ in $V_{\tilde C_0}$ would make a two-dimensional section infinitely far from its cone, contradicting Claim 5.8.

nodes.name: Build a planar section from the offending vector
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some vector $w\in \tilde Z$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$. Then $\IR_+w\subset \tilde Z$. Pick any vector $v\in q^{-1}(w)\subset Z$ and consider the two-dimensional subspace $Z_2=\lin(\{v,e\})$ spanning the vectors $v$ and $e$. Observe that for every $t\in\IR$ we get $f_i(v+te)=\tilde f_i(w)>0$, which implies that $(v+t\IR)\cap V_{Z_2\cap C}=\emptyset$. Then $V_{Z_2\cap C}\subset \IR e-\bar\IR_+v$ and $q(V_{Z_2\cap C})\subset -\bar\IR_+w$.
